title: Permalist Project
summary: Guided project: turn an in-memory to-do list (Express, EJS, body-parser) into a persistent one backed by a Postgres table called items, implementing all four CRUD operations with the pg package. The lecture explains the starter code, sets the brief, then walks through the finished solution route by route.

concepts.heading: What the project is and the starting point
points: Permalist is a to-do list whose items survive refreshes and server restarts because they live in Postgres, not in a JavaScript array.
Download Permalist Project.zip from the lesson resources, extract it, and open it in VS Code. It already includes the styling, icons and EJS views (with header and footer partials).

Starter index.js keeps items in a plain array. Run it with npm i then nodemon index.js and open localhost:3000. Adding an item works, but restarting the server resets the array, because RAM-held data disappears with the process. That is the problem Postgres solves here.
In the starter, the /edit and /delete routes exist as forms in the front end but the server does nothing with them yet.
Suggested time: roughly one to two hours, with more thinking than typing.

concepts.heading: Understanding the front end before coding
points: index.ejs loops over listItems and renders one row per item: a checkbox form (delete), a paragraph with the title, an edit form, and an edit button.
The delete form posts to /delete. Its checkbox has name deleteItemId and value set to the item's id, and an onchange handler that submits the form as soon as the box is ticked.

The edit form posts to /edit. It has two inputs: a hidden one named updatedItemId carrying the item's id, and a text input named updatedItemTitle prefilled with the current title via EJS, so the user edits rather than retypes.

The text input and the done button start hidden. A small browser script, handler(id), is called by the pencil button: it hides the paragraph and edit button and reveals the input and done button, so the title visually becomes an editable field. This script has nothing to do with persistence.
The add form has a text input named newItem and posts to /add.
body-parser (urlencoded, extended: true) turns these form fields into req.body.<name> on the server. Knowing exactly which name each form sends is the key to writing the routes.

concepts.heading: Database setup
points: Create a database called permalist (pgAdmin: right-click Databases, Create, Database, Save).

Inside it create table items with id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY (auto-incrementing whole number that identifies each row) and title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL (max 100 characters; NOT NULL blocks rows without a title, an optional safeguard for later error checking).
Optionally seed two rows matching the array in the starter (Buy milk, Finish homework). The table could equally start empty and be filled through the app.
queries.sql in the project holds this schema if stuck, but the suggestion is to attempt it from earlier lessons first.
The provided solution.js only runs if names match: database permalist, table items, columns id and title.

concepts.heading: Read: connect and select
points: Import pg (already listed in package.json with body-parser, ejs and express) and create new pg.Client with user, host, database, password and port. Same settings as previous projects except database is now permalist; a wrong database name is the usual connection failure. Then call db.connect().

In app.get('/'), inside try/catch, await db.query('SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY id ASC'), assign result.rows to items, and pass it to res.render('index.ejs', { listTitle: 'Today', listItems: items }).
result.rows is an array of objects, one per row, with column names as keys (here id and title). Logging it with console.log is the recommended way to inspect it.
ORDER BY id ASC is optional but useful: without it Postgres may return an edited row at the end, so items jump around after an update. Sorting by id keeps the original order.
Error handling is basic in this project: log the error in catch.

concepts.heading: Create: the /add route
points: The server reads the new text from req.body.newItem.

It runs db.query('INSERT INTO items (title) VALUES ($1)', [item]). The $1 placeholder is filled from the array in the second argument (parameterised query). id is generated by SERIAL, so only title is supplied.
After the insert, res.redirect('/'). The redirect makes the browser request the home route again, which re-queries the database and re-renders the page, effectively refreshing it with the new row.
Errors are caught and logged. The earlier items.push line from the in-memory version is no longer needed.

concepts.heading: Update: the /edit route
points: Clicking the pencil swaps the paragraph for the prefilled input; submitting with the done button posts updatedItemTitle and updatedItemId to /edit.

The route reads both fields from req.body, then runs db.query('UPDATE items SET title = ($1) WHERE id = $2', [item, id]). Order of the values array must match the numbering: $1 is the new title, $2 the id.
The id travels through a hidden input because the browser shows only the title, but the server has to know which row to change.
Redirect to '/' afterwards, log any error.

concepts.heading: Delete: the /delete route
points: Ticking the checkbox fires onchange, which submits its form, POSTing deleteItemId (the row's id) to /delete.
The route reads req.body.deleteItemId and runs db.query('DELETE FROM items WHERE id = $1', [id]), then redirects to '/'.
WHERE id = $1 is essential so only that row is removed.

concepts.heading: Upgrade ideas given
points: Sort by creation date: add a column with ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, store a date from JavaScript or the database, and show it.
Several lists (for example Today, This week, This month, or Work and School), which implies a lists table and a relationship between lists and items.
A family to-do list where different users own different chores, reusing the user pattern from the Family Travel Tracker.
The project is a common interview exercise, so adding a personal improvement helps it stand out.

task.name: Permalist: persist a to-do list in Postgres with full CRUD
task.starting_point: Permalist Project.zip: index.js (in-memory array version), views/index.ejs plus header/footer partials, public/styles and icon assets, package.json (express, ejs, body-parser, pg), and queries.sql. The page renders and adds items to the array, but edit and delete do nothing and data is lost on restart.
task.goal: Replace the array with a Postgres database so items can be created, read, edited and deleted and the list survives refreshes and server restarts.
steps: Read index.js and index.ejs first. Note the names each form sends: newItem (/add), updatedItemTitle plus updatedItemId (/edit), deleteItemId (/delete), and how the handler function toggles the edit UI.
Run npm i, then nodemon index.js, and check localhost:3000 works with the array. Restart the server to see the data reset.
Create table items with id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY and title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL. Optionally insert 'Buy milk' and 'Finish homework'.
In index.js import pg, create a pg.Client configured for the permalist database, and call connect().
GET /: query all rows ordered by id, store result.rows in items, and render index.ejs with listTitle and listItems.
POST /add: insert req.body.newItem as a new title with a parameterised query, then redirect to '/'.
POST /edit: update title where id matches, using req.body.updatedItemTitle and req.body.updatedItemId, then redirect.
POST /delete: delete the row whose id equals req.body.deleteItemId, then redirect.
Test each action, restart the server and refresh to confirm the data persists. Optionally compare with solution.js, or attempt an upgrade.
task.expected_result: A working to-do list: items listed from the database in id order, new items appear after adding, the pencil lets you rename an item and save it, ticking the checkbox removes it, and everything is still there after restarting the server.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.16 - Permalist Project/ (index.js, solution.js, queries.sql, views/index.ejs)

pitfalls: Wrong database name in the pg.Client config (still world or another earlier project) stops the app connecting.
The values array order must match $1, $2 in the UPDATE; swapping them writes the id into the title or updates nothing.
Forgetting res.redirect('/') leaves the request hanging, and the page does not refresh with the new data.
Without ORDER BY the list can reorder after an update.
Form field names in the EJS (newItem, updatedItemTitle, updatedItemId, deleteItemId) must match what the route reads from req.body.
Leaving out WHERE on the UPDATE or DELETE would change or remove every row.

Reference repo note: its index.js already contains the finished solution and is identical to solution.js, and it holds a hard-coded local password; use your own and keep it out of version control. (Extra)
(Extra) Only unhandled errors are logged, so a failed query leaves the browser waiting; add a res.status(500) response for production use.

gaps_and_ideas: New project lesson 'Permalist: persistent to-do list' with a blurb about CRUD with Postgres, Express and pg.

Tasks: (1) create the permalist database and items table, (2) wire GET / to SELECT with ORDER BY id, (3) implement /add with a parameterised INSERT, (4) implement /edit with UPDATE and the hidden id, (5) implement /delete from the checkbox form; stretch: add a created_at column via ALTER TABLE.
Starter code idea: provide the in-memory index.js and the EJS from the course, with TODO comments where the db.query calls go.

Interactive demo idea: a side-by-side view of the form POST, the SQL statement it triggers with the $1/$2 values filled in, and the resulting table rows, updated as the user adds, edits and ticks items.
Worth showing: why redirect after POST re-runs the GET query, and what happens to the data when the server restarts in the array version versus the database version.
